newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Senate sees six-week interim budget approved.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Senate sees six-week interim budget approved.

text.p: The New York Senate Majority Leader said he expected a six-week, interim budget to be approved before the present one expires on Friday, a measure that is needed because negotiators still are far fairly apart.
"We're going to get back together some time on Wednesday, probably in the morning, pass the emergency bill, I hope on Wedensday, and we have general agreement on that," said Joseph Bruno, R-Troy.
Bruno spoke with reporters after the first major meeting by lawmakers in two weeks, as the legislature had adjourned for a two-week, spring break.

He added that questions about a proposal to extend two expired taxes, one that helps supports the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and a bank tax, had complicated talks over the interim budget. "So the counsel's going to look at that, but I don't think it was a real difference of opinion on the substance," he told reporters.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, again urged the Senate to approve its own version of a budget, which was due on April 1. Such tardiness is not unusual for the state, as this is the 13th year in a row that lawmakers have failed to agree on time a budget. A fight over rent controls, which expire on June 15 and which mainly affect New York City, is one of the main issues that is stalling the budget talks, but the subject was only discussed in passing, according to Bruno.

Silver, noting both the Democrat-led Assembly and the Republican governor had put forward their own budgets, said the Senate was deliberately keeping its stand vague. "They don't want to do it; they don't want to show the public where they disagree with the governor or with us."

He added: "We really have no understanding of where they are in terms of cuts to health care, in terms of cuts to higher education, whether they are for the restoration of the proposed cuts in the form of increased tuition at our state university system, or cuts to the various programs that make up the system," he told reporters. He said finding out where the Senate stood on such specific items would speed talks.
